expectedText:
S CORPORATION ELECTION OVERVIEW
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ELIGIBILITY
Acme, Inc. can qualify to elect S corporation tax treatment only if it meets the federal 'small business corporation' test: a domestic corporation that isn't a bank, insurance company, or certain other ineligible corporation, and that doesn't have more than 100 shareholders, doesn't have a shareholder that isn't an individual (other than certain estates and trusts), doesn't have a nonresident alien as a shareholder, and doesn't have more than one class of stock.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "the term “small business corporation” means a domestic corporation which is not an ineligible corporation and which does not— (A) have more than 100 shareholders, (B) have as a shareholder a person (other than an estate, a trust described in subsection (c)(2), or an organization described in subsection (c)(6)) who is not an individual, (C) have a nonresident alien as a shareholder, and (D) have more than 1 class of stock."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, small business corporation eligibility test (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  Known gap: The 100-shareholder count isn't a strict headcount of every person who owns stock — federal law treats all members of a single family, and their estates, as one shareholder for this purpose, which can make the practical limit much higher than 100 individual people. This document doesn't state which businesses would actually benefit from S corporation treatment — that depends on income level, how owners are paid, and other facts specific to the business. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific eligibility test separately.

COUNTING SHAREHOLDERS: THE FAMILY RULE
The 100-shareholder cap doesn't count every stockholder individually: a husband and wife (and their estates) count as one shareholder, and so does an entire family — a common ancestor plus that ancestor's lineal descendants and their spouses or former spouses — no matter how many of them actually hold stock. There's a limit to how far back the family line can be traced for this purpose: an individual doesn't count as the common ancestor if, as of the relevant date, they're more than six generations removed from the youngest generation of shareholders who would otherwise be treated as part of the family.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(A), there shall be treated as one shareholder— (i) a husband and wife (and their estates), and (ii) all members of a family (and their estates)."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(A)-(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, members of a family treated as one shareholder (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  "The term “members of a family” means a common ancestor, any lineal descendant of such common ancestor, and any spouse or former spouse of such common ancestor or any such lineal descendant."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, who counts as a member of the family (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  "An individual shall not be considered to be a common ancestor if, on the applicable date, the individual is more than 6 generations removed from the youngest generation of shareholders who would (but for this subparagraph) be members of the family."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(1)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the six-generation limit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. It only addresses how shareholders are counted toward the 100-shareholder cap — it doesn't change who is eligible to be a shareholder at all (the separate rules on individuals, estates, trusts, and nonresident aliens still apply).

WHAT DOESN'T COUNT AS A SECOND CLASS OF STOCK
Two structures common in small corporations don't by themselves violate the one-class-of-stock eligibility rule: giving some shares more voting power than others while keeping the same economic rights (for example, voting and non-voting common stock), and straight debt — a written, unconditional promise to pay a fixed sum on demand or on a set date, where the interest rate and payment dates aren't tied to profits, the borrower's discretion, or similar factors, that isn't convertible into stock, and that's held by someone eligible to be an S corporation shareholder (or a bank or similar lender in the ordinary course of lending).

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(D), a corporation shall not be treated as having more than 1 class of stock solely because there are differences in voting rights among the shares of common stock."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, voting-rights differences among common stock disregarded (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  "For purposes of subsection (b)(1)(D), straight debt shall not be treated as a second class of stock."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(5)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, straight debt safe harbor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  "For purposes of this paragraph, the term “straight debt” means any written unconditional promise to pay on demand or on a specified date a sum certain in money if— (i) the interest rate (and interest payment dates) are not contingent on profits, the borrower’s discretion, or similar factors, (ii) there is no convertibility (directly or indirectly) into stock, and (iii) the creditor is an individual (other than a nonresident alien), an estate, a trust described in paragraph (2), or a person which is actively and regularly engaged in the business of lending money."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1361(c)(5)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the full definition of straight debt (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1361)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text.

SHAREHOLDER CONSENT
An S corporation election is only valid if every person who is a shareholder on the day the election is made consents to it.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "An election under this subsection shall be valid only if all persons who are shareholders in such corporation on the day on which such election is made consent to such election."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, unanimous shareholder consent requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  Known gap: This is a real, all-or-nothing requirement — a single non-consenting shareholder can block the election entirely, no matter how small that shareholder's stake is. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific consent requirement separately.

WHEN THE ELECTION MUST BE MADE
Acme, Inc. can make an S corporation election either at any time during the tax year before the one it's meant to take effect for, or during that tax year itself, as long as it's made by the 15th day of the third month of that tax year.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "An election under subsection (a) may be made by a small business corporation for any taxable year— (A) at any time during the preceding taxable year, or (B) at any time during the taxable year and on or before the 15th day of the 3d month of the taxable year."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, S corporation election timing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  Known gap: Missing this deadline doesn't necessarily end the option — the IRS has authority to accept a late election where there was reasonable cause for the delay, though that relief isn't automatic and this document doesn't state what qualifies as reasonable cause. Absent such relief, an election made after the deadline is instead treated as made for the following tax year. This is one federal rule; no additional independent source was found restating this specific deadline separately.

REVOKING THE ELECTION
Unlike making the election in the first place, which requires every shareholder's consent, revoking it takes less: shareholders holding more than half of Acme, Inc.'s shares, as of the day the revocation is made, is enough to consent to revoke. Timing controls when it takes effect: a revocation made by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year is effective retroactively to the start of that same tax year; made any later, it's effective starting the following tax year instead — unless the revocation itself specifies a later, prospective effective date, in which case that specified date controls.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "An election may be revoked only if shareholders holding more than one-half of the shares of stock of the corporation on the day on which the revocation is made consent to the revocation."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, revocation requires more than half of shares, not unanimity (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "a revocation made during the taxable year and on or before the 15th day of the 3d month thereof shall be effective on the 1st day of such taxable year, and (ii) a revocation made during the taxable year but after such 15th day shall be effective on the 1st day of the following taxable year."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, when a revocation takes effect (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "If the revocation specifies a date for revocation which is on or after the day on which the revocation is made, the revocation shall be effective on and after the date so specified."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, a revocation may instead specify a prospective date (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. This asymmetry is real and worth noticing: unanimous consent is required to elect S status, but only a bare majority is required to end it — a minority shareholder who wants to keep S status has no statutory veto over a majority's decision to revoke it.

AN INVOLUNTARY TERMINATION TRAP
S status can also end without anyone voting to end it. If Acme, Inc. has accumulated earnings and profits (which generally means it was previously a C corporation, or acquired one, and never distributed out its retained C-corporation earnings) at the close of each of three consecutive tax years, and more than 25% of its gross receipts in each of those same three years comes from passive investment income — royalties, rents, dividends, interest, and annuities — the S election terminates automatically, effective the first day of the tax year after that third consecutive year.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "An election under subsection (a) shall be terminated whenever the corporation— (I) has accumulated earnings and profits at the close of each of 3 consecutive taxable years, and (II) has gross receipts for each of such taxable years more than 25 percent of which are passive investment income."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, automatic termination for excess passive income with accumulated earnings and profits (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "Any termination under this paragraph shall be effective on and after the first day of the first taxable year beginning after the third consecutive taxable year referred to in clause (i)."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(d)(3)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, when this termination becomes effective (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. This trap doesn't apply to an S corporation that has never had C-corporation earnings and profits to begin with — a company that has been an S corporation from its first tax year, and has no accumulated E&P from before that election, can't trigger this specific termination path no matter how passive its income is.

IF S STATUS ENDS — FIXING IT OR WAITING IT OUT
If S status is lost — whether by revocation, by ceasing to qualify, or by the passive-income trap above — two different paths exist depending on the cause. If the loss happened by genuine accident (a missed shareholder consent, an eligibility slip the corporation didn't realize), the IRS can treat the corporation as having remained an S corporation the whole time, if it determines the circumstances were inadvertent, the corporation fixes the underlying problem within a reasonable time after discovering it, and the corporation and every affected shareholder agree to make whatever tax adjustments the IRS requires. Absent that relief, once an election has been terminated, the corporation generally can't re-elect S status again until its fifth tax year after the one the termination took effect in — a five-year wait — unless the IRS consents to an earlier re-election.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "the Secretary determines that the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination were inadvertent"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — the IRS's determination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "no later than a reasonable period of time after discovery of the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination, steps were taken— (A) so that the corporation for which the election was made or the termination occurred is a small business corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be, or (B) to acquire the required shareholder consents"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — fixing the problem (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "the corporation for which the election was made or the termination occurred, and each person who was a shareholder in such corporation at any time during the period specified pursuant to this subsection, agrees to make such adjustments (consistent with the treatment of such corporation as an S corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be) as may be required by the Secretary with respect to such period"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f)(4) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — shareholder agreement to adjustments (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "then, notwithstanding the circumstances resulting in such ineffectiveness or termination, such corporation shall be treated as an S corporation or a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, as the case may be, during the period specified by the Secretary."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(f) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, inadvertent termination relief — the actual outcome (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  "such corporation (and any successor corporation) shall not be eligible to make an election under subsection (a) for any taxable year before its 5th taxable year which begins after the 1st taxable year for which such termination is effective, unless the Secretary consents to such election."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1362(g) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, the five-year bar on re-electing after termination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1362)
  Known gap: This is one federal rule, verified against the current U.S. Code text. Inadvertent-termination relief is a determination the IRS makes on the specific facts, not something a corporation can grant itself by simply asserting good faith; this document doesn't state what the IRS actually looks for in making that determination.

HOW TO FILE
The election is made by filing IRS Form 2553, signed by an authorized corporate officer, with the shareholder consents required above attached or included on the form. Form 2553 is filed with the IRS — it is a federal tax filing, not a state filing, and it doesn't replace or change anything filed with Acme, Inc.'s state of incorporation or organization.

CONSENT SIGNATURES
Consent to this election:

Shareholder: _______________________ Date: _______________
Shareholder: _______________________ Date: _______________
(Every shareholder on the date of the election must consent. Add additional lines as needed.)
